2256.idn: Ginyanga (self-designation of speakers: anyanga), North Guang, Kwa; glottocode giny1241, ISO ayg; data: Agbandi (largest Anyanga village), Prefecture of Blitta, Central Togo; consultants from Agbandi and Diguina; four field trips 2019-2024 (five months total); corpus collected 2019-2024
2256.tone: Two level tones H and L; TBU = a single vowel (vowel sequences are biphonemic, each vowel its own TBU, cf. PFV prefix ɔ̀ɔ́-); syllabic nasal /n/ bears tone (ń- 1sg.IPFV H vs ǹ- cl6 L). Tone is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs 15-16) and grammatically contrastive (IPFV H prefix vs PFV L-H prefix). The sketch says nothing about stress, accent, prominence or rhythm; 'prominence' occurs only for discourse prominence (focus markers, sec. 3.8). Sister sources say the same or less: Aplonova 2025 PhD sec. 2.1.2 p. 31 ('Ginyanga has two phonological tones: high and low... A tone bearing unit contains only one vowel... The nasal /n/ bears tones when it is followed by a consonant'), prosody of complex predicates explicitly 'non analysee'; Pozdniakova & Aplonova 2024 ('Ginyanga is a tonal language, with two structural tones'); Pozdniakova & Aplonova 2022 p. 244 ('Ginyanga is a tonal language that has presumably high and low phonemic level tones'); Pozdniakova 2021 fn. 1 (tonal language like other Kwa languages, tone system understudied, examples untonemarked). No source denies word stress, so this is 'tone system, no stress rule', not no word stress.

2257.prule: Fixed word-level penultimate accent whose exponent is vowel length: the vowel of the penultimate syllable of every word unit is noticeably longer than all others and demarcates the word ('accent (i.e. the penultimate syllable)'); quantity-insensitive (no phonemic vowel-length contrast, length has no grammatical or semantic function). Dynamic stress on the penult is explicitly not characteristic of giTonga (an individual idiosyncrasy); stress proper has only expressive 'characteristic' uses (final syllable of distal demonstratives).

2260.prule: None stated. Goemai is a tone language (H, L, contour HL; underlying LH on a few items). Word stress ('prosodic prominence') is recognised, but the grammar declares its placement inadequately understood; the only generalisation is a tendency for stress to fall on high-tone syllables. A stressed open syllable can occur in any position within the word (it is lengthened and never reduced to schwa); short unstressed vowels of polysyllabic words reduce to schwa, most often in the initial CV syllable.

2260.tone: Tone language: two level tones H and L and one contour tone HL (falling), HL mostly on long vowels; an underlying LH on a few items (subject pronouns, some nouns/verbs/TAM markers) never surfaces on one syllable but spreads its H to the first syllable of the next word (Tabain & Hellwig 2015 p. 90; Hellwig 2011 p. 66 summary excerpt: 'Goemai has two level tones (high, low) and one contour tone (falling)'). On stress: Hellwig 2011 p. 51 says stress patterns are inadequately understood and need further research, and that stress tends to fall on high-tone syllables (citing Burquest 1971 on Angas); p. 61 and JIPA p. 87: a stressed open syllable, in any word position, is realized long and never as schwa (schwa -> [ɔː]); p. 60 / JIPA p. 92: short non-stressed vowels of polysyllabic words reduce to [ə], the commonest vowel of the initial CV syllable in CV.CV(V)(C) words. Raised pitch register of H tones in presentative constructions is an intonational adjustment, not stress. Clause-final open syllables are also lengthened and clause-final H becomes falling (p. 65 excerpt), a boundary effect distinct from stress.

(ii) the application of metrical production rules. In that case the stressed syllable is preserved but because elision has taken place it shifts ... 'ata 'eke > 'a'teke 'that man'
2264.heavy: No syllable-weight condition is stated; the conditioning is the presence and position of onset consonants ('the syllable introduced by the second last consonant'; 'except where there is no such consonant').
2264.dflt: first syllable ('except where there is no such consonant when the stress falls on the first syllable')
2264.prule: Non-verb roots: 1-2 syllables always initial; 3 syllables: stress the syllable 'introduced by the second last consonant' (i.e. whose onset is the root's second-last consonant), initial when there is no such consonant; 4+ syllables: initial stress plus stress on the second-last-consonant syllable (two stresses, unranked). For all-CV roots this yields penult (2: 10, 3: 010, 4: 1010, 5: 10010) but onsetless syllables shift it leftward ('baeka, 'arai, 'aefa vs a'kuba, a'teki), so the position is fixed by consonant position, not by syllable count or weight. Unaffected by suffixes/enclitics on non-verbs.
2264.srule: Two stresses per long word, same mark, not ranked primary vs secondary: non-verb roots of 4+ syllables take stress on the first syllable and on the syllable introduced by the second-last consonant ('auki'horo, 'avana'deri; exception 'dekui'eku); inflected verbs take root-initial stress plus stress on the syllable containing the second-last consonant of the form ('mane'mima, 'manemeri'hero). 2266.prule: No general word-stress rule for simplex words is stated anywhere in the reachable sources. ter Laan 1953 states stress ('klem') only for morphologically complex words: ordinary determinative compounds, including adjective+noun compounds that express one concept (doodlid, nijboer, grootknecht), carry main stress on the first member; the characteristically Gronings copulative 'koppelingen' (aartenbonen, hozenvouten, koppenoren, spekkenaaier) always carry it on the second member; compound place names ('t Hooghoes, Graauwdiek) on the final member, except Nijstad; the suffix -achteg is stressed when it means 'having' (dailachteg, woonachteg; also reusachteg) but the first member is stressed when it means 'resembling' (geelachteg, kinderachteg); Romance loans keep unstressed i (muzikant, foabrikant, pp.168-169). Simplex-word stress is presupposed to be as in Dutch (Reker 2002:50 on onverstandeg: 'net als in het Nederlands het belangrijkste accent op de voorlaatste lettergreep'; clipped onverstand, antam, baloor 'alle met de nadruk op de eerste lettergreep').

2268.dq: at the level of the phonological word, the parameter for prominence is set to the left. The result is that in a fully composed phonological word, it is the leftmost foot which is prominent. [...] surface-level stress in Wanano is ultimately assigned at the level of the phonological word, but is the cumulative product of parameters set at the levels of syllables and feet.
2268.dloc: ch. 2, sec. 2.3.3 'Stress assignment', 2.3.3.1 (pp. 73-75) and 2.3.3.2 'Foot parameters' (pp. 76-77); sec. 2.5.1 'Tone or Pitch-Accent?' p. 83; sec. 2.5.2 p. 85; sec. 2.5.3 (closing restrictions) p. 92
2268.heavy: None: 'Due to this ‘no-coda’ restriction, it is not possible to formulate rules by which weight is assigned to syllables according to the shape of the rhyme. [...] Therefore, weight is not product of syllable shape in Wanano and must be based on other features of the prosodic structure: mora and foot-level parameters.' (p. 73); each nucleus = one mora, no contrastive vowel length.
2268.prule: Stress falls on the final syllable of the root: roots (always the leftmost constituent of the phonological word, overwhelmingly bimoraic CV.CV / CV.V, c. 60 monosyllabic roots lengthened to CV.V) form a right-headed foot, suffixes form weak monomoraic feet, and word-level prominence goes to the leftmost foot, so the root-final syllable (normally the second syllable of the word) is stressed whatever the number of suffixes; e.g. die-ro-re [dierore] 'to the dog' stressed on the root-final -e. Syllable shape/rhyme weight plays no role ('weight is not product of syllable shape in Wanano'); syllables of the exceptional glottal-coda shape (C)Vʔ (the only coda allowed, e.g. the first syllable of ~si'di [siʔ.ni] 'drink', du'te 'chop') are never stressed.
2268.srule: Existence reported, placement not given. Stenzel 2004 states no secondary-stress rule (suffixes are weak monomoraic feet, non-prominent at word level; one prominent foot = the root); she reports Waltz & Waltz 2000:455 that 'A H tone associated with any secondary accents within a phonological word is automatically lowered, as there is only one allowable H tone per phonological word' (p. 83). Waltz 2007:5 likewise: secondary accents follow the primary, are weaker ('la segunda parte de una palabra fonológica se disminuye'), and are marked per entry; no positional rule.

2268.tone: Stenzel 2004 sec. 2.5 treats pitch as suprasegmental lexical tone: 'Noun and verb roots are always lexically marked with a tonal melody, whereas suffixes are nearly always unmarked for tone' (p. 85); two underlying melodies H and HL with an optional extrametrical initial L, minimal pairs at (36) p. 88 (su'a LH/LHL, tua LH/H, toa H/HL, yoa H/LH); melody of the head root spreads rightward to the end of the phonological word. Waltz's description (H vs L, accent on the first H syllable, one H per word) is noted to match Hyman's pitch-accent prototype, but 'It is still unclear whether or not the pitch-accent model adequately describes the patterns found in Wanano and other ET languages; so, for now, I will refer to the Wanano system as tonal' (p. 84). Stenzel 2005 (Portuguese, in the copy consulted) restates the same: four melodies BAB, BA, AB, A and 'a associacao de um tom A (ou ‘acento’) a uma dessas moras, normalmente a segunda' (root bimoraic, H normally on the second mora). Note the tension the source does not resolve: the less frequent H and HL root classes have H on the root-initial mora, and since the first H 'co-occurs with stress' those roots would have root-initial prominence; this is presumably what 'in the great majority of cases' hedges.

tn.quote: Gomez-Imbert identifies four surface tonal patterns: H, HL, LH and LHL, which reduce to two underlying contrastive tonal melodies: H and HL, with the classification of any initial L as a default, extrametrical tone … Thus, the possible tonal melodies can be understood as (<L>)H, and (<L>)HL … Each tonal element is associated one-to-one from left to right to a mora, identified as the tone-bearing unit. … Noun and verb roots are always lexically marked with a tonal melody, whereas suffixes are nearly always unmarked for tone, and are thus targets for tonal spread.

tn.locator: ch. 2 sec. 2.5.2 'Tonal melodies and basic association', pp. 84-85; surface restrictions at end of 2.5.3, p. 92
tn.note: Roots carry a lexical melody H or HL, often with an initial low (surface H, HL, LH, LHL), one tone per mora, spread rightward over the word; separate root-final stress is aligned with the first H.

2272.prule: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable of the word. Stated explicitly for the Gugu-Badhun dialect (sec. 3.2 'Word Stress', p.82) of what Sutton calls the 'Upper Burdekin River Dialects' (Warungu, Gugu-Badhun, Gudjal; sec. 2.2, p.30). 2273.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Guduf (with Cinene and Glavda, all from the author's own 1999/2001 fieldwork) is described as having two register tones, H and L, transcribed impressionistically, with weak pitch salience and a low functional load; no vowel-length contrast; 'stress phenomena' appear only in some morpho-syntactic environments (e.g. the plural suffix {-́xà}) and are 'on the whole not common'. 2273.quote: <초분절요소> 어휘의 채록 과정에서 일부 단어에서 고성조를 가진 모음이 약간 길게 발음되는 경우가 있었지만 이러한 장모음이 변별적 기능을 갖는 경우는 발견할 수 없었다. 강세 현상도 일부 형태-통사적 환경(예: 복수 접미사 {-́xà})에서 나타나기는 하지만 전반적으로 흔하지는 않다. 이와 같은 현상들은 세 언어 모두 공통적이라고 할 수 있다. 어휘 목록에서 보다시피 모든 단어에 대해 성조가 표시되어 있는데 이는 단순히 본 연구자가 직접 청취한대로 전사한 결과로서 아직 성조의 기능적 실체를 정확히 밝혀내지는 못했다. 그 이유는 청각적으로 고성조와 저성조 간의 높낮이가 하우사어나 요루바어와 같은 다른 전형적인 성조어들처럼 그다지 뚜렷하지 않은데다가 또한 채록된 언어자료에서 성조가 변별적 기능을 하는 환경들을 아직 발견하지 못했기 때문이다. 그러나 현재까지의 분석 결과를 놓고 볼 때 이 세 언어 모두에서 성조의 기능적 부담(functional load)은 그리 크지 않은 것으로 보인다.

2273.idn: Cited work is a sketch of Cinene [cine1238], but its §3 summarises the author's own 1999/2001 field data on Cinene, Glavda AND Guduf, and the §3.1 suprasegmental statement (<초분절요소>: H/L tone of low functional load; stress only marginal) is said by the author to hold for all three languages…
2273.tone: Kim 2010 pp. 140-141: H and L tone marked on every word in the word list 'simply as the researcher heard it'; the H/L pitch difference is not as clear as in Hausa or Yoruba; no environment in which tone is distinctive has yet been found; functional load of tone in all three languages (Cinene, Glavda, Guduf) 'does not appear to be great'. Kim 2009 report pp. 11-12 (the Guduf sentence and fn. 5 on p. 12) adds, of the same finding: '이는 비단 치네네, 글라브다어뿐만 아니라 본 연구자의 박사논문으로써 비교적 연구가 많이 진행된 구두프어도 마찬가지이다' (this holds not only for Cinene and Glavda but equally for Guduf, comparatively well studied as the subject of my doctoral thesis) and fn. 5: '구두프어에는 고성조와 저성조가 있는데 지금까지 밝혀진 바로는 이들 성조의 어휘나 문법 변별 기능이 극히 제한적인 것으로 나타났다' (Guduf has a high and a low tone, but as far as established so far their lexical or grammatical distinctive function has proved extremely limited). Kim 2006 p. 40, Guduf-specific: '(3) 성조 / 장단: 두 개의 성조가 구분되지만(고성조 á, 저성조 à), 그 기능 부담성은 상대적으로 약함. 따라서 표기법에서는 표시하지 않음. 모음의 장단 구분 없음.' (Two tones are distinguished, H á and L à, but their functional load is relatively weak, so they are not written in the orthography; no vowel-length contrast.) Stress: 'stress phenomena' only in some morpho-syntactic environments (plural suffix), uncommon; no accent rule.

2274.dq: Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que lleva el acento prosódico. Esta sílaba está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra. ... En el amuzgo, la sílaba acentuada es generalmente la última sílaba del tema.
2274.prule: Every word has exactly one stressed syllable, pronounced with greater intensity; it is the last syllable of the stem (tema). quantity-insensitive. Enclitic dependent pronouns (=ya, =na, =yoꞌ...) and the animate enclitic =ñe that follow the root are unstressed, so stress stays on the last root/stem syllable before them; a word-final dependent adverb (part of the predicate stem) carries the stress. Apóstol Polanco 2024 (acoustic: duration, F0, intensity): 'el acento es fijo y final en el AX dentro de la raíz'; foot type iambic; stress stays on the last root at the end of the base under affixation and cliticization.
2274.srule: None: 'Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que lleva el acento prosódico... se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra' (one stress per word, stem-final; no secondary or rhythmic stress described). Secondary stress is likewise not mentioned in Do Bui 2018 ch. 2, de Jesús García 2019 §5.12 or Apóstol Polanco 2024 §6.3.

2274.tone: Tone language, independent of stress. Buck 2018 §2.4.4 p. 23: 'Cada sílaba de las palabras amuzgas se pronuncia con su propio tono. Hay niveles de tonalidad alto, medio y bajo; y también hay deslices. Los tonos de las sílabas controladas tienden a deslizar hacia arriba ligeramente; los tonos de las sílabas balísticas tienden a deslizar hacia abajo.' (Cuadro 5: alto, medio, bajo, deslices alto-bajo, medio-alto, bajo-medio). Stress is described separately as intensity (§2.4.2), and §2.4.3 says the ballistic/controlled syllable differences 'se notan más en las sílabas acentuadas'. Apóstol Polanco 2024 measures duration, F0 and intensity as stress correlates and reports the full vowel-length/phonation/nasality/tone contrasts only in the tonic (final root) syllable; Do Bui 2018 counts 5 tones. Not tone or pitch accent: an explicit, fixed word-stress rule coexists with lexical tone.

2275.dq: It should be noted here that the rules of morphophonemic changes of vowel nuclei and tone (2.3 and 3.2) affect only the stressed (final) syllable of a compound verb stem. ... Syllabic enclitics are set off by a hyphen, indicating that they are secondarily stressed syllables. (The units described are the verb word 'aspect + STEM + bound subject + bound object', p. 43, and noun compounds; no phrase…
2275.prule: Primary stress is anchored to the stem (root): simple stems are monosyllabic and stressed; in a compound stem the final element carries the stress and every preceding syllable is 'prestressed' (unstressed, with nucleus and tone neutralized); aspect prefixes precede the stressed stem and syllabic person enclitics follow it with only secondary stress. Stress is therefore located by morphological constituency (the stem-final syllable), not counted from a word edge: e.g. gʷdàhgʷ-yáhk-mè 'they ate' (stem + two secondarily stressed enclitic syllables), gácǒʔ-mè 'he is working' (syllabic aspect prefix + stressed stem + enclitic).
2275.srule: Secondary stress on syllabic person enclitics after the stem: 'Syllabic enclitics are set off by a hyphen, indicating that they are secondarily stressed syllables' (p. 81); 3pl -yáhk stands 'in a non-final, secondarily stressed syllable' before -mé, e.g. gʷdàhgʷ-yáhk-mè 'they ate' (p. 82). Placement is morphological, not rhythmic; pre-stem syllables are unstressed.
2275.quote: 2.1. Simple stems are always monosyllabic in GHZ. Compound stems tend to be bisyllabic, but it is not always possible to determine the meaning of both of the syllable, although the second syllable is usually recognizable. The reason for this is that there is a general rule of neutralization in GHZ which simplifies the syllable nucleus of all prestressed syllables. Tones are neutralized to high tone in prestressed syllables across morpheme boundaries (e.g., in compounds). ... Another type of compounding is that of the verb stem plus the morpheme -nǒ Acompaniment/Instrument or a stative verb st…
2275.idn: Guevea de Humboldt Zapotec (GHZ), 'this dialect of Zapotec' spoken at Guevea de Humboldt, Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico
2275.tone: GHZ has three tones, 'high, low and rising' (note 1, p. 83b), plus nucleus types V, Vʔ, Vh. Tone and nucleus contrasts are carried by stressed (and secondarily stressed) syllables; in prestressed syllables 'tones are neutralized to high tone' and the nucleus is simplified (p. 51). The paper uses stress terminology throughout ('prestressed', 'stressed (final) syllable', 'secondarily stressed'), so this is a stress-plus-tone system, not a tone-only one.

2276.dloc: §5 Conclusions, p. 191, items a)-c) (Rosetta Project excerpt, archive.org)
2276.prule: No stress or accent rule is stated. The authors' own summary of the prosodic system of Guibéroua Bété is exclusively tonal: four distinctive level tone registers, a stable tone system, no contour tones; syllables may have a two-mora centre (CVV, ClV) in which the syllabic liquid bears its own distinctive tone. Words accent, accentuation, intensité, stress occur nowhere in the six held excerpts (pp. 5-7, 82, 85, 150-153, 191-203, 214-215 + bibliography), and the table of contents (pp. 214-215) has no accent section (only 1.1 Segments et tons, 1.1.1 La notation de more, 1.1.2 Oppositions des tonèmes, 1.1.3 Réalisation des tonèmes, 1.2.5 Note sur le mot phonologique).

Stress not discussed in the source. The tonal reading is what the authors themselves put under 'système prosodique'. Consistent secondary evidence: WALS 13A codes Bété (source Werle-and-Gbalehi-1976) as 'complex tone system' with no 14A-17A stress values (per this entry's source list).

2277.prule: Stress is predictable and morphologically determined: in every inflected word it falls on the root (radical); in compounds of two or three roots it falls on the syllable of the last root; no affix ever bears stress. Since roots are predominantly monosyllabic and polysyllables arise only by affixation or compounding (§2.1), the stressed syllable is the (last) root syllable wherever it sits, i.e. final in prefix+root verbs but non-final when suffixes/enclitics follow.

tn.quote: Au bout du compte, les données toléraient mieux l'analyse du pòŋààl comme langue à tons, c'est-à-dire une langue dans laquelle chaque syllabe est dotée de hauteur (relative) déterminée. Dans cette langue, la syllabe se définit elle-même comme unité tonale. … 3-4 Deux hauteurs pertinentes. La transcription phonétique d'énoncés met en évidence quatre registres de hauteur ponctuelle. L'examen des documents permet d'avancer que deux hauteurs seulement interviennent de manière significative: ce sont les deux « tons » dits haut et bas.
tn.translation: In the end, the data better tolerated the analysis of pòŋààl as a tone language, i.e. a language in which each syllable is endowed with a determined (relative) pitch. In this language the syllable itself is defined as the tonal unit. … 3-4 Two relevant pitches. The phonetic transcription of utterances shows four registers of level pitch. Examination of the documents allows one to state that only two pitches intervene significantly: these are the two 'tones' called high and low.
tn.cite: Pairault, Claude. 1969. Documents du parler d'Iro, kùláál du Tchad. Paris: Librairie C. Klincksieck (Langues et littératures de l'Afrique noire, 5). 285 pp.
tn.locator: Ch. 3 'Prosodie', sec. 3-3 end pp. 50-51 and sec. 3-4 p. 51
tn.note: Two tones, high and low, every syllable a tonal unit; rising and falling pitch on long vowels reduced to sequences of the two levels; intensity non-distinctive. The author doubted this in 1994.

2281.dq: Where the root takes prefixes, the first syllable of the prefix, or series of prefixes, takes secondary stress (shown here as ˝): ˝ŋu-´warbaɻ -ɟi-n '1MinS-bright, light-Thmsr-Fut: I'll be bright'
2281.dloc: Ch. 1, section 1.2.2 'Stress', thesis p. 18; apparent exceptions, loans and stress shift pp. 18-20.
2281.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (root-initial), regardless of how many prefix syllables precede it; prefixes do not otherwise carry primary stress, except that before the monosyllabic root wu 'give' primary stress falls on the final syllable -bu- of a di- or polysyllabic prefix (a´bu-wu-ni, but ˝ŋu-´wu-ni), and before zero-suffixed ni 'sit' (Precontemporary / Irrealis 2) it may shift to the final syllable of the pronominal prefix. In unprefixed simple words this is word-initial; in prefixed words primary stress sits word-internally at the root edge. In compounds and reduplications primary stress goes to the first syllable of the first root (reduplications always), but many lexicalised compounds/derived verbs place it on the first syllable of the second root instead, sometimes optionally. No weight conditioning is stated.
2281.srule: In prefixed words the first syllable of the prefix (or of the prefix string) bears secondary stress, primary stress staying on the root-initial syllable. In compound and reduplicated stems the first syllable of the root that does not bear primary stress bears secondary stress (normally the second root; in many compounds the first root, with primary on the second; in compound verbs the left member, the verb root keeping primary stress). Secondary stress is placed by morphological constituent; no rhythmic/alternating secondary stress within roots is described.

2282.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word; quantity-insensitive (contrastive vowel length is itself confined to initial syllables, p.195, so length cannot compete with the initial position). 2282.srule: Not mentioned in Black 1980 (Sec. 4 'Phonologies of the attested languages', Kurtjar subsection, pp.194-196 read in full; the only stress statement is predictable first-syllable stress, p.196).
